topic: Argo CD: syncing and the Application

notes.front: What does an automated sync policy let Argo CD do?
notes.back: Sync an application automatically when it detects differences between the desired manifests in Git and the live state in the cluster.
notes.explanation: Without it, a sync waits for someone to start it.
notes.example: Like a thermostat set to “auto” rather than a heater you switch on by hand.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automated Sync Policy”
notes.evidence: Argo CD has the ability to automatically sync an application when it detects differences between the desired manifests in Git, and the live state in the cluster.

notes.front: What are sync options in Argo CD?
notes.back: Settings that customise some aspects of how Argo CD syncs the desired state into the target cluster.
notes.explanation: Most are set in the Application’s `spec.syncPolicy.syncOptions`; some can be set as annotations on a single resource.
notes.example: Like the settings on a copier: the same job, but single- or double-sided.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Options”, “Sync Options”
notes.evidence: Argo CD allows users to customize some aspects of how it syncs the desired state in the target cluster. Some Sync Options can be defined as annotations in a specific resource. Most of the Sync Options are configured in the Application resource `spec.syncPolicy.syncOptions` attribute.

notes.front: In Argo CD, what is a resource hook, and how is a resource made into one?
notes.back: A resource assigned to a sync phase with the `argocd.argoproj.io/hook` annotation, so it is applied at a set point, such as before the main sync.
notes.explanation: During a sync, Argo CD applies the resource in the phase the annotation names.
notes.example: Like a pre-flight checklist: a step that must happen at a fixed point before take-off.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “Sync Phases and Waves”
notes.evidence: Adding the argocd.argoproj.io/hook annotation to a resource will assign it to a specific phase. During a Sync operation, Argo CD will apply the resource during the appropriate phase of the deployment.

notes.front: What are PreDelete and PostDelete hooks?
notes.back: Hooks that run when an Application is deleted: PreDelete before its resources are deleted, PostDelete after all of them are deleted.
notes.explanation: They belong to deleting the Application, not to its syncs.
notes.example: Like backing up a room before it is cleared, and sending a “done” note once it is empty.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, hook types table; “PreDelete and PostDelete Hooks”
notes.evidence: Executes before Application resources are deleted.

notes.front: What is a sync wave in Argo CD?
notes.back: An integer set with the `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave` annotation that orders resources: Argo CD deploys from the lowest number to the highest.
notes.explanation: It is another way of changing the sync order, besides phases.
notes.example: Like boarding groups on a plane: group 1 boards before group 2.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “How sync waves work?”
notes.evidence: They are defined by the argocd.argoproj.io/sync-wave annotation. The value is an integer that defines the ordering (ArgoCD will start deploying from the lowest number and finish with the highest number).

notes.front: What is a selective sync (also called a partial sync)?
notes.back: A sync in which only some of the application’s resources are synced.
notes.explanation: You choose which resources in the web interface or the command-line tool.
notes.example: Like saving only the pages you changed rather than the whole document.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Selective Sync”, “Selective Sync”
notes.evidence: is one where only some resources are sync'd. You can choose which resources from the UI or the CLI:

notes.front: What are sync windows in Argo CD?
notes.back: Configurable windows of time in which syncs are either blocked or allowed.
notes.explanation: A window has a kind (allow or deny), a cron-format schedule and a duration.
notes.example: Like a shop’s opening hours for deployments.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Windows”, “Sync Windows”
notes.evidence: Sync windows are configurable windows of time where syncs will either be blocked or allowed. These are defined by a kind, which can be either `allow` or `deny`, a `schedule` in cron format and a duration

notes.front: What is commit pinning in Argo CD?
notes.back: Giving a Git commit hash as the revision, so the app is pinned to the manifests at that commit.
notes.explanation: The documentation calls it the most restrictive tracking technique.
notes.example: Like citing a book by its exact edition rather than “the latest printing”.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Tracking and Deployment Strategies”, “Commit Pinning”
notes.evidence: If a Git commit SHA is specified, the app is effectively pinned to the manifests defined at the specified commit. This is the most restrictive of the techniques

notes.front: In an Application spec, what does `source` refer to?
notes.back: The desired state in Git: repository, revision, path and environment.
notes.explanation: It is one of the two key pieces of information that define an Application.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Declarative Setup”, “Applications”
notes.evidence: `source` reference to the desired state in Git (repository, revision, path, environment)

notes.front: In an Application spec, what does `destination` refer to?
notes.back: The target cluster and namespace.
notes.explanation: Source says what to deploy; destination says where.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Declarative Setup”, “Applications”
notes.evidence: `destination` reference to the target cluster and namespace.

notes.front: An Application’s `destination` sets both `server: https://kubernetes.default.svc` and `name: in-cluster`. What happens?
notes.back: B: it results in an error.
notes.choices:
A) Argo CD uses `server` and ignores `name`
B) It results in an error
C) Argo CD deploys to both
notes.choicesExplained: A and C: the cluster may be given by server or by name, but not both.
notes.explanation: Setting both is not allowed.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Declarative Setup”, “Applications”
notes.evidence: For the cluster one of server or name can be used, but not both (which will result in an error).

notes.front: With automated sync, how does a CI/CD pipeline deploy, and what access does it no longer need?
notes.back: It commits and pushes manifest changes to the tracked Git repository; it no longer needs direct access to the Argo CD API server.
notes.explanation: The documentation names this as a benefit of automatic sync.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automated Sync Policy”
notes.evidence: A benefit of automatic sync is that CI/CD pipelines no longer need direct access to the Argo CD API server to perform the deployment. Instead, the pipeline makes a commit and push to the Git repository with the changes to the manifests in the tracking Git repo.

notes.front: Your security team wants the build pipeline to have no access to Argo CD at all; it may only push to Git. Which setting lets deployments still happen?
notes.back: An automated sync policy on the Application.
notes.explanation: With automatic sync, the pipeline makes a commit and push and Argo CD deploys the change.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automated Sync Policy”
notes.evidence: CI/CD pipelines no longer need direct access to the Argo CD API server to perform the deployment.

notes.front: What is the difference between manual and automated sync?
notes.back: Manual: someone starts each sync. Automated: Argo CD syncs by itself when it detects differences between Git and the live state.
notes.explanation: Automated sync is switched on with `argocd app set <APPNAME> --sync-policy automated` or an `automated` sync policy.
notes.contrast: Who starts the sync: a person, or Argo CD on detecting a difference.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automated Sync Policy”
notes.evidence: Argo CD has the ability to automatically sync an application when it detects differences between the desired manifests in Git, and the live state in the cluster.

notes.front: By default, does automated sync delete a resource that is no longer defined in Git?
notes.back: No. Set `prune: true` in the automated policy (or `--auto-prune`), or run a manual sync with pruning.
notes.explanation: The documentation calls the default a safety mechanism.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automatic Pruning”
notes.evidence: By default (and as a safety mechanism), automated sync will not delete resources when Argo CD detects the resource is no longer defined in Git. To prune the resources, a manual sync can always be performed (with pruning checked).

notes.front: An app has automated sync with default settings. You delete `old-worker.yaml` from Git. The Deployment it defined is still running an hour later. Why?
notes.back: C: automated sync does not prune by default.
notes.choices:
A) Automated sync only runs once a day
B) The Deployment is Degraded
C) Automated sync does not prune by default
notes.choicesExplained: A: the interval is minutes, not a day. B: health has nothing to do with pruning.
notes.explanation: Pruning needs the prune option in the automated sync policy, or a manual sync with pruning checked.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automatic Pruning”
notes.evidence: Pruning can also be enabled to happen automatically as part of the automated sync by running:

notes.front: With automated sync and prune on, what does Argo CD protect against by default, and which option removes that protection?
notes.back: It prevents an application from having no target resources (an empty application). `allowEmpty: true` (or `--allow-empty`) allows it.
notes.explanation: The protection is against automation or human errors.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automatic Pruning with Allow-Empty (v1.8)”
notes.evidence: By default (and as a safety mechanism), automated sync with prune have a protection from any automation/human errors when there are no target resources. It prevents application from having empty resources.

notes.front: By default, do changes made directly to the live cluster trigger an automated sync?
notes.back: No. They do only if `selfHeal` is set to true (or `--self-heal`).
notes.explanation: Self-heal enables automatic sync when the live state deviates from the state in Git.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automatic Self-Healing”
notes.evidence: By default, changes that are made to the live cluster will not trigger automated sync. To enable automatic sync when the live cluster's state deviates from the state defined in Git, run:

notes.front: Automated sync is on (no other options). Someone edits a ConfigMap in the cluster by hand. Git has not changed. What does Argo CD do automatically?
notes.back: B: nothing. The app shows OutOfSync, but no automated sync runs unless `selfHeal` is true.
notes.choices:
A) Reverts the change at once
B) Nothing; it needs `selfHeal: true` to sync on live changes
C) Deletes the ConfigMap
notes.choicesExplained: A would need self-heal. C: nothing here deletes resources.
notes.explanation: Changes made to the live cluster do not trigger automated sync by default.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automatic Self-Healing”
notes.evidence: By default, changes that are made to the live cluster will not trigger automated sync.

notes.front: With `selfHeal` set to true, a sync is attempted again after the self-heal timeout, which is {{c1::5 seconds}} by default.
notes.explanation: The timeout is set by the `--self-heal-timeout-seconds` flag of the application controller.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automated Sync Semantics”
notes.evidence: If the `selfHeal` flag is set to true, then the sync will be attempted again after self-heal timeout (5 seconds by default) which is controlled by `--self-heal-timeout-seconds` flag of `argocd-application-controller` deployment.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Argo docs as of that date

notes.front: When will an automated sync be performed?
notes.back: Only if the application is OutOfSync. Synced applications, or applications in an error state, will not attempt it.
notes.explanation: The first rule of the automated sync semantics.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automated Sync Semantics”
notes.evidence: An automated sync will only be performed if the application is OutOfSync. Applications in a Synced or error state will not attempt automated sync.

notes.front: An app with automated sync shows Synced but Degraded. Will automated sync run to fix the health?
notes.back: No. Automated sync runs only when the app is OutOfSync.
notes.explanation: Automated sync reacts to sync status, not health: an app that is Synced is left alone even while it is Degraded.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automated Sync Semantics”
notes.evidence: An automated sync will only be performed if the application is OutOfSync.

notes.front: How many automated sync attempts does Argo CD make per commit?
notes.back: One per unique combination of commit and application parameters (unless `selfHeal` is true).
notes.explanation: If the most recent successful sync already used that commit and those parameters, no second sync is attempted.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automated Sync Semantics”
notes.evidence: Automated sync will only attempt one synchronization per unique combination of commit SHA1 and application parameters.

notes.front: An automated sync against commit `a1b2c3` failed. Nothing has changed since, and no retry is configured. Will Argo CD try that sync again?
notes.back: No. Automatic sync does not reattempt after a failed attempt against the same commit and parameters.
notes.explanation: A new commit, or new parameters, would allow a fresh attempt.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automated Sync Semantics”
notes.evidence: Automatic sync will not reattempt a sync if the previous sync attempt against the same commit-SHA and parameters had failed.

notes.front: The automatic sync interval comes from `timeout.reconciliation` in the `argocd-cm` ConfigMap, which defaults to {{c1::`120s`}}, with added jitter of `60s`.
notes.explanation: With the jitter, the maximum period is 3 minutes.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automated Sync Semantics”
notes.evidence: which defaults to `120s` with added jitter of `60s` for a maximum period of 3 minutes.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Argo docs as of that date

notes.front: You push a commit to an app with automated sync and default settings, and no webhook is set up. At most, how long before the automatic sync check comes round?
notes.back: About 3 minutes: 120 seconds plus up to 60 seconds of jitter.
notes.explanation: The interval is `timeout.reconciliation`, whose default gives a maximum period of 3 minutes.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automated Sync Semantics”
notes.evidence: The automatic sync interval is determined by the timeout.reconciliation value in the argocd-cm ConfigMap , which defaults to `120s` with added jitter of `60s` for a maximum period of 3 minutes.
notes.validAsOf: 2026-09-25 · Argo docs as of that date

notes.front: How can Argo CD retry a failed sync, and what `limit` value gives unlimited retries?
notes.back: With the `retry` field of the sync policy, using exponential backoff; `-1` means unlimited.
notes.explanation: `backoff.factor` multiplies the wait after each failed attempt.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Automated Sync Policy”, “Automatic Retry with a limit”
notes.evidence: Argo CD can automatically retry a failed sync operation using exponential backoff. To enable, configure the `retry` field in the sync policy:

notes.front: How do you give one resource several sync options through its annotation?
notes.back: Join them with a comma in the `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options` annotation value.
notes.explanation: White space around the comma is trimmed.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Options”, “Sync Options”
notes.evidence: Multiple Sync Options which are configured with the `argocd.argoproj.io/sync-options` annotation can be concatenated with a `,` in the annotation value; white-space will be trimmed.

notes.front: A resource carries the sync option `Prune=false`, but the Application’s sync policy prunes. Which wins?
notes.back: The resource’s `Prune=false`: a Prune option on the resource always overrides the Application’s policy.
notes.explanation: The app will show out of sync if Argo CD expects the resource to be pruned.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Options”, “No Prune Resources”
notes.evidence: Note that setting a Prune sync option on the resource will always override a Prune sync policy defined in the Application.

notes.front: Both `ApplyOutOfSyncOnly=true` and a selective sync apply only some resources. What is the difference?
notes.back: With `ApplyOutOfSyncOnly`, sync hooks still run and the sync is recorded in history. A selective sync does neither.
notes.explanation: By default a sync applies every object, which is slow for applications with thousands of objects.
notes.contrast: History and hooks: kept with ApplyOutOfSyncOnly, lost with selective sync.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Options”, “Apply Resources OutOfSync Only”
notes.evidence: Unlike Selective Sync , when `ApplyOutOfSyncOnly` is enabled, Sync Hooks will still run and the sync will be recorded in the history.

notes.front: What does the `PruneLast=true` sync option do?
notes.back: Makes pruning a final, implicit wave of the sync, after other resources are deployed and healthy and all other waves have succeeded.
notes.explanation: It can be set for the whole Application or on a single resource.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Options”, “Prune Last”
notes.evidence: This feature is to allow the ability for resource pruning to happen as a final, implicit wave of a sync operation, after the other resources have been deployed and become healthy, and after all other waves completed successfully.

notes.front: With `Replace=true`, which commands does Argo CD use to apply changes, and what is the risk?
notes.back: `kubectl replace` or `kubectl create`. It can be destructive: resources may be recreated, which could cause an outage.
notes.explanation: The default is `kubectl apply`.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Options”, “Replace Resource Instead Of Applying Changes”
notes.evidence: This sync option has the potential to be destructive and might lead to resources having to be recreated, which could cause an outage for your application.

notes.front: A resource is too big for the 262144-byte annotation limit that client-side `kubectl apply` relies on. Which sync option avoids this?
notes.back: `ServerSideApply=true`.
notes.explanation: Server-side apply does not use the annotation.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Options”, “Server-Side Apply”
notes.evidence: Resource is too big to fit in 262144 bytes allowed annotation size. In this case server-side apply can be used to avoid this issue as the annotation is not used in this case.

notes.front: Without `CreateNamespace=true`, what happens if an Application’s destination namespace does not exist?
notes.back: The Application fails to sync.
notes.explanation: With the option, Argo CD creates the namespace named in `spec.destination.namespace`.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Options”, “Create Namespace”
notes.evidence: Without this either declared in the Application manifest or passed in the CLI via `--sync-option CreateNamespace=true`, the Application will fail to sync if the namespace doesn't exist.

notes.front: A new Application targets the `billing` namespace, which nobody has created. What should you add so the first sync succeeds?
notes.back: The sync option `CreateNamespace=true`.
notes.explanation: It makes Argo CD create the namespace in `spec.destination.namespace` if it does not already exist.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Options”, “Create Namespace”
notes.evidence: The example above shows how an Argo CD Application can be configured so it will create the namespace specified in `spec.destination.namespace` if it doesn't exist already.

notes.front: What kinds of Kubernetes resources can be hooks?
notes.back: Any kind, but they tend to be Pods, Jobs or Argo Workflows.
notes.explanation: Several hook types can be given as a comma-separated list.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “Sync Phases and Waves”
notes.evidence: Hooks can be any type of Kubernetes resource kind, but tend to be Pod, Job or Argo Workflows. Multiple hooks can be specified as a comma separated list.

notes.front: Which hook type executes before the manifests are applied?
notes.back: `PreSync`.
notes.explanation: If any PreSync hook fails, the whole sync stops and is marked as failed.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, hook types table
notes.evidence: Executes prior to the application of the manifests.

notes.front: Which hook type executes after all PreSync hooks have succeeded, at the same time as the manifests are applied?
notes.back: `Sync`.
notes.explanation: It runs alongside the main application of the manifests.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, hook types table
notes.evidence: Executes after all `PreSync` hooks completed and were successful, at the same time as the application of the manifests.

notes.front: Which hook type tells Argo CD not to apply the manifest at all?
notes.back: `Skip`.
notes.explanation: Resources marked Skip are not applied.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, hook types table
notes.evidence: Indicates to Argo CD to skip the application of the manifest.

notes.front: Which hook type executes after all Sync hooks succeed, the application succeeds and all resources are Healthy?
notes.back: `PostSync`.
notes.explanation: It waits for health as well as for the Sync hooks.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, hook types table
notes.evidence: Executes after all `Sync` hooks completed and were successful, a successful application, and all resources in a `Healthy` state.

notes.front: Which hook type executes when the sync operation fails?
notes.back: `SyncFail`.
notes.explanation: SyncFail hooks can be used for clean-up and other housekeeping; if one fails, Argo CD only marks the operation as failed.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, hook types table
notes.evidence: Executes when the sync operation fails.

notes.front: Before each deployment you must confirm the database is reachable, and stop the deployment if it is not. Which hook type fits?
notes.back: A: `PreSync`.
notes.choices:
A) PreSync
B) PostSync
C) SyncFail
notes.choicesExplained: B runs after the manifests are applied, too late to stop them. C runs only once a sync has already failed.
notes.explanation: If a PreSync hook fails, the whole sync stops and is marked as failed.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “How phases work?”
notes.evidence: Apply all the resources marked as PreSync hooks. If any of them fails the whole sync process will stop and will be marked as failed

notes.front: Does a PreDelete hook run when a sync prunes resources?
notes.back: No. It runs only when the Application itself is being deleted.
notes.explanation: Normal sync operations do not run it, even when pruning is enabled.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “PreDelete Hooks”
notes.evidence: They run only during Application deletion (e.g., `kubectl delete application` or `argocd app delete`), not during normal sync operations, even when pruning is enabled.

notes.front: What happens to an Application’s deletion if its PreDelete hook fails?
notes.back: Deletion is blocked: the Application stays deleting with a `DeletionError` condition, and its resources are not deleted.
notes.explanation: Fixing the hook in Git, or deleting the failing hook resource, lets the deletion go ahead.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “PreDelete Hooks”
notes.evidence: If a PreDelete hook fails (e.g., a Job fails or a Pod crashes), the Application deletion is blocked:

notes.front: Which hook deletion policy deletes the hook resource when the sync succeeds?
notes.back: `HookSucceeded`.
notes.explanation: The policy is set with the `argocd.argoproj.io/hook-delete-policy` annotation.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “Hook lifecycle and cleanup”
notes.evidence: The hook resource is deleted when the sync succeeds.

notes.front: Which hook deletion policy deletes the hook resource after the hook failed?
notes.back: `HookFailed`.
notes.explanation: It is the counterpart of HookSucceeded.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “Hook lifecycle and cleanup”
notes.evidence: The hook resource is deleted after the hook failed.

notes.front: Which hook deletion policy deletes any existing hook resource before the new one is created, and is assumed when none is set?
notes.back: `BeforeHookCreation`.
notes.explanation: It is meant to be used with a fixed `/metadata/name`.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “Hook lifecycle and cleanup”
notes.evidence: Note that if no deletion policy is specified, Argo CD will automatically assume `BeforeHookCreation` rules.

notes.front: You want a migration hook Job removed when the sync succeeds, but kept for debugging when it fails. Which deletion policy do you set?
notes.back: `HookSucceeded`.
notes.explanation: It deletes the hook only when the sync succeeds; HookFailed would do the opposite.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “Hook lifecycle and cleanup”
notes.evidence: The hook resource is deleted when the sync succeeds.

notes.front: What sync wave are hooks and resources in by default, and can a wave be negative?
notes.back: Wave 0. Yes, a wave can be negative, to run before all other resources.
notes.explanation: A negative wave comes before the default wave 0.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “How sync waves work?”
notes.evidence: Hooks and resources are assigned to wave 0 by default. The wave can be negative, so you can create a wave that runs before all other resources.

notes.front: When a sync starts, Argo CD orders resources by phase, then by wave, then by {{c1::kind}}, then by name.
notes.explanation: Kind puts namespaces first, then other Kubernetes resources, then custom resources.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “Combining Sync waves and hooks”
notes.evidence: By kind (e.g. namespaces first and then other Kubernetes resources, followed by custom resources)

notes.front: In one sync phase: a Secret with no wave annotation, a Deployment at wave `2`, and a Job at wave `-1`. In what order are they applied?
notes.back: The Job (−1), then the Secret (0), then the Deployment (2).
notes.explanation: Waves go from lowest to highest, and a resource with no annotation is in wave 0.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “How sync waves work?”
notes.evidence: Order all resources according to their wave (lowest to highest)

notes.front: In what wave order does Argo CD prune resources?
notes.back: In reverse: resources in higher waves are pruned first.
notes.explanation: If pruning in a wave fails, lower waves are not processed.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “How phases work?”
notes.evidence: During pruning, the wave order is reversed from the creation order. Resources in higher waves are pruned first.

notes.front: After a selective sync, can you roll back to it?
notes.back: No. A selective sync is not recorded in the history, so rollback is not possible.
notes.explanation: Rollback works from the sync history.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Selective Sync”, “Selective Sync”
notes.evidence: Your sync is **not** recorded in the history, and so rollback is not possible.

notes.front: Do resource hooks run during a selective sync?
notes.back: No.
notes.explanation: The selective sync page gives the same warning.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Phases and Waves”, “How phases work?”
notes.evidence: Hooks do not run during a selective sync operation.

notes.front: Can one Application be affected by several sync windows, and one window apply to several Applications?
notes.back: Yes to both: the relationship is many-to-many.
notes.explanation: A window selects Applications by name, cluster or namespace.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Sync Windows”, “Relationship between Sync Windows and Applications”
notes.evidence: The relationship between Sync Windows and Application resources is many-to-many. This means that an Application resource may be affected by multiple Sync Windows, and that a single Sync Window definition may apply to multiple Application resources.

notes.front: Which finalizer makes deleting an Application also delete its resources (a cascading delete)?
notes.back: `resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io`.
notes.explanation: With it, the application controller performs the cascading delete.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “App Deletion”, “About The Deletion Finalizer”
notes.evidence: When deleting an Application with this finalizer, the Argo CD application controller will perform a cascading delete of the Application's resources.

notes.front: Without the `resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io` finalizer, what happens to managed resources when you delete the Application?
notes.back: They are not deleted; only the Application goes.
notes.explanation: A cascading delete needs the finalizer.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Declarative Setup”, “Applications”
notes.evidence: Without the `resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io` finalizer, deleting an application will not delete the resources it manages. To perform a cascading delete, you must add the finalizer.

notes.front: You will delete an Application with `kubectl delete app`, and you want its Deployments and Services removed too. What must be set first?
notes.back: The `resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io` finalizer on the Application.
notes.explanation: For a cascade delete with kubectl, set the finalizer, for example with `kubectl patch`.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “App Deletion”, “Deletion Using kubectl”
notes.evidence: To perform a cascade delete set the finalizer, e.g. using `kubectl patch`:

notes.front: What is the difference between a cascade and a non-cascade delete of an Application?
notes.back: A cascade delete removes the app and its resources. A non-cascade delete (`--cascade=false`) removes only the app.
notes.explanation: `argocd app delete APPNAME` without flags performs a cascade delete.
notes.contrast: Cascade takes the resources with it; non-cascade leaves them running.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “App Deletion”, “App Deletion”; “Deletion Using argocd”
notes.evidence: Apps can be deleted with or without a cascade option. A **cascade delete**, deletes both the app and its resources, rather than only the app.

notes.front: What is the default propagation policy for a cascading Application delete, and which finalizer gives the alternative?
notes.back: Foreground. `resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io/background` gives background cascading deletion.
notes.explanation: The policy can also be set with `--propagation-policy`.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “App Deletion”, “About The Deletion Finalizer”
notes.evidence: Argo CD performs background cascading deletion when `resources-finalizer.argocd.argoproj.io/background` is set.

notes.front: If an Application tracks a branch, what does Argo CD compare the live state against?
notes.back: The manifests at the tip of that branch.
notes.explanation: To redeploy, commit and push a manifest change to the tracked branch.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Tracking and Deployment Strategies”, “HEAD or branch tracking”
notes.evidence: If a branch name or a symbolic reference (like HEAD) is specified, Argo CD will continually compare live state against the resource manifests defined at the tip of the specified branch

notes.front: An Application tracks a Git tag. How do you redeploy it with different manifests?
notes.back: Retag: move the tag to a different commit.
notes.explanation: A tag is generally considered more stable than a branch, and less frequently updated.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Tracking and Deployment Strategies”, “Tag Tracking”
notes.evidence: To redeploy an app, the user uses Git to change the meaning of a tag by retagging it to a different commit SHA.

notes.front: Production is pinned to a commit. A fix is merged to `main`. What must happen for production to get it?
notes.back: C: update the Application’s tracked revision to a commit containing the fix.
notes.choices:
A) Nothing; Argo CD picks up the new commit on its own
B) Retag the pinned commit
C) Update the Application’s revision to a commit containing the fix
notes.choicesExplained: A: a pinned app does not follow the branch. B: commits cannot change meaning, unlike tags.
notes.explanation: Updating the tracked revision is the only way to change a pinned app’s live state.
notes.source: Argo CD documentation, “Tracking and Deployment Strategies”, “Commit Pinning”
notes.evidence: Since commit SHAs cannot change meaning, the only way to change the live state of an app which is pinned to a commit, is by updating the tracking revision in the application to a different commit containing the new manifests.
